title: How Deep Is the Control? Lie-Bracket Depth–Width Trade-offs, the Generic Bias of Learned Models, and a Negative Result on Structural Priors
content: A system with m controlled channels and a drift can reach all d directions of its state space either by having many channels or by composing a few of them in time through Lie brackets. We ask how that trade-o is quantied, whether noise limits how much temporal composition is usable, and, nally, whether a model learned from data reveals the bracket depth of the system that produced the data. What we prove. Writing r = m + 1 for the number of generating elds, bracket depth obeys an exact counting lower bound δLB (d, r) given by Witt's formula, and this bound is attained for every (d, r) (a restatement of facts about free nilpotent Lie algebras). No universal upper bound exists: two generators can require depth d − 2. Our main theoretical addition is that, inside any nite-dimensional polynomial family and for any absolutely continuous prior on its coecients, almost every tuple of elds has depth exactly δLB . This predicts that a learned control-ane model, being a typical draw, will sit at δLB (deff , r) whatever the true system is. What we measure. On designed systems the algebra is visible: σmin ∝ T k+1 holds on seven testbeds with t R 2 = 1.000; the number of usable bracket levels under open-loop noise ε grows like c ln(1/ε) with a slope c that depends on segment duration (we give a heuristic that reproduces the measured values to within roughly 10%); and feedback adds one to three levels. On learned models the picture is less attering to the estimator: pure neural control-ane ts land on δLB for all four testbeds where we ran them, bilinear ts recover the truth only when the model class contains it (2/4 testbeds), and on four real cortical sessions the tted depth equals δLB but also equals the matched null, so the real- data test is inconclusive. The H-JEPA measurement is limited to an eective dimension (deff ≈ 75); depth itself was not measured. What did not work. A gradient-level bracket-injector prior meant to push a learner above δLB succeeds on one of four testbeds (trivially); we report three failure modes and analyse them from the loss denition. A test of whether nonlinear additive drift lowers depth did not measure Lie depth reliably and is reported as inconclusive. Takeaway. Where the model class cannot express a system's bracket structure, the depth one reads o a tted model is a property of the learner (deff , m, function class), not of the system. Detecting real Lie structure from data will need either structured model classes or estimators calibrated against matched nulls.
